theme: Food, rice & sleep · 먹는 것과 건강

tracks.title: What should you eat for a better night's sleep?

transcript.speaker: Phil
transcript.text: Hi Georgie.

transcript.speaker: Georgie
transcript.text: Hi Phil.

transcript.speaker: Georgie
transcript.text: Now, Phil, do you ever struggle to get a good night's sleep?

transcript.speaker: Phil
transcript.text: You know, I do sometimes.

transcript.speaker: Phil
transcript.text: If I've been thinking about something a lot, or even worse, if I've had a cup of coffee later than I should, sometimes I can lie there for hours.

transcript.speaker: Georgie
transcript.text: Yes.

transcript.speaker: Georgie
transcript.text: Well, many of us will be familiar with that feeling of lying in bed, feeling really tired, but just not being able to go to sleep, but what causes us to struggle to sleep and is there anything we can do about it?

transcript.speaker: Georgie
transcript.text: Well, researchers have for a while been interested in the link between what we eat and how we sleep.

transcript.speaker: Georgie
transcript.text: Today on 6 Minute English, we'll be talking about this and asking, "What should you eat for a better night's sleep?"

transcript.speaker: Georgie
transcript.text: OK.

transcript.speaker: Georgie
transcript.text: Phil, let's start with a quiz question.

transcript.speaker: Georgie
transcript.text: So, adults need between 7–9 hours sleep a night to stay healthy, according to experts, but what percentage of people in the UK say they get less than this?

transcript.speaker: Phil
transcript.text: OK.

transcript.speaker: Phil
transcript.text: I think people find sleeping hard, so I think it's going to be c) 35%.

transcript.speaker: Georgie
transcript.text: OK.

transcript.speaker: Georgie
transcript.text: Well, we'll find out the answer later in the programme.

transcript.speaker: Phil
transcript.text: Georgie, you've been looking at the research on this.

transcript.speaker: Phil
transcript.text: Do scientists think that what we eat affects how we sleep?

transcript.speaker: Georgie
transcript.text: Yes, they do.

transcript.speaker: Georgie
transcript.text: Scientists have done some long-term studies.

transcript.speaker: Georgie
transcript.text: So, looking at large groups of people over a long period of time, and they found that a healthier diet is associated with better quality sleep.

transcript.speaker: Georgie
transcript.text: They've also done some smaller studies looking in more detail at exactly what people are eating and then studying how they sleep in a laboratory.

transcript.speaker: Phil
transcript.text: OK.

transcript.speaker: Phil
transcript.text: And in these studies, have they found that particular foods are better for our sleep than others?

transcript.speaker: Georgie
transcript.text: Well, it's less about particular foods and more about particular nutrients.

transcript.speaker: Georgie
transcript.text: So, nutrients means important things your body needs to survive and be healthy.

transcript.speaker: Georgie
transcript.text: For example, protein is a nutrient.

transcript.speaker: Georgie
transcript.text: BBC World Service programme The Food Chain has been speaking to researcher Professor Marie-Pierre St-Onge about which nutrients are important for sleep.

transcript.speaker: Marie-Pierre St-Onge
transcript.text: So, diets that look more like a Mediterranean pattern – higher in fruits and vegetables, whole grains, lower in animal-based foods, lower in sugar.

transcript.speaker: Marie-Pierre St-Onge
transcript.text: But then from our own research, where we evaluate food intakes in the lab, we see different... similar patterns, really.

transcript.speaker: Marie-Pierre St-Onge
transcript.text: But when we talk about nutrients, diets that are higher in fibre, which we find in fruits and vegetables and whole grains, and lower in saturated fats, which we find in more plant-based types of foods, are associated with more deep sleep at night.

transcript.speaker: Georgie
transcript.text: Marie-Pierre says that Mediterranean-style diets are associated with good sleep.

transcript.speaker: Georgie
transcript.text: A Mediterranean diet includes lots of vegetables and less animal-based foods such as meat and dairy.

transcript.speaker: Phil
transcript.text: Yes, and Marie-Pierre's own research shows that some nutrients, such as fibre, are important for sleep and others, such as saturated fats, are less important.

transcript.speaker: Phil
transcript.text: Saturated fat is a type of fat mainly found in meat and dairy that's thought to be bad for your health.

transcript.speaker: Georgie
transcript.text: Right.

transcript.speaker: Georgie
transcript.text: And according to Marie-Pierre, eating less saturated fat and more nutrients like fibre is associated with more deep sleep at night.

transcript.speaker: Georgie
transcript.text: A deep sleep is when you are more fully asleep and your body is able to rest.

transcript.speaker: Phil
transcript.text: So, Georgie, it sounds like thinking about our diets is important if we want to improve our sleep.

transcript.speaker: Phil
transcript.text: And now I've heard that certain foods have a lot of nutrients that can be helpful for sleep.

transcript.speaker: Phil
transcript.text: Is that true?

transcript.speaker: Georgie
transcript.text: Well, there is some limited research on specific foods and their impact on sleep.

transcript.speaker: Georgie
transcript.text: So, for example, scientists have been studying kiwi fruits and also tart cherry juice.

transcript.speaker: Georgie
transcript.text: And you may also see adverts for supplements that claim to improve sleep.

transcript.speaker: Georgie
transcript.text: Supplements are tablets you take, which contain particular nutrients that you might not get in your everyday diet.

transcript.speaker: Georgie
transcript.text: But experts say that focusing on our whole diet, rather than one particular fruit or supplement, is going to be the most effective.

transcript.speaker: Georgie
transcript.text: Here's sleep doctor Allie Hare explaining more to BBC World Service programme The Food Chain.

transcript.speaker: Allie Hare
transcript.text: I think people are looking for the one supplement often or the... you know, we're fed a lot of these things, aren't we, on social media?

transcript.speaker: Allie Hare
transcript.text: This magical powder or this magical tablet that you can take that will, you know, help you sleep better immediately from tonight.

transcript.speaker: Allie Hare
transcript.text: And of course, you know, Marie-Pierre and I know that there is no such magic bullet, unfortunately.

transcript.speaker: Allie Hare
transcript.text: And if there was, I'm sure, you know, we would be... we would be doing very well for ourselves.

transcript.speaker: Phil
transcript.text: Allie says people are looking for a supplement that can help them sleep.

transcript.speaker: Georgie
transcript.text: Yes.

transcript.speaker: Georgie
transcript.text: She says we are fed information on social media about magical tablets.

transcript.speaker: Georgie
transcript.text: If you are fed information, you are given lots of it in a continuous way.

transcript.speaker: Phil
transcript.text: But Allie argues that experts know there's no magic bullet to help you sleep, and a magic bullet refers to a simple and effective solution to a problem that's usually one that doesn't exist.

transcript.speaker: Phil
transcript.text: OK.

transcript.speaker: Phil
transcript.text: Well, now I think it's time to find out the answer to your quiz question, Georgie.

transcript.speaker: Georgie
transcript.text: Yes.

transcript.speaker: Georgie
transcript.text: I asked you what percentage of UK adults say they get less than seven hours sleep a night.

transcript.speaker: Phil
transcript.text: And I said I thought it was c) 35%.

transcript.speaker: Georgie
transcript.text: You are correct, Phil.

transcript.speaker: Georgie
transcript.text: Yes, 35% of adults say they get six hours or less sleep a night, according to a study by YouGov.

transcript.speaker: Georgie
transcript.text: OK.

transcript.speaker: Georgie
transcript.text: Let's recap the vocabulary we learned in this programme, starting with nutrients, which are important things your body needs to survive and be healthy.

transcript.speaker: Phil
transcript.text: Saturated fats are fats mainly found in meat and dairy products that are thought to be bad for our health.

transcript.speaker: Georgie
transcript.text: A deep sleep is when your body is fully asleep and able to rest.

transcript.speaker: Phil
transcript.text: Supplements are tablets or other things which contain particular nutrients you might not get in your everyday diet.

transcript.speaker: Georgie
transcript.text: To feed information means to give lots of it in a continuous way.

transcript.speaker: Phil
transcript.text: And a magic bullet is a simple and effective solution, and it's often one that doesn't exist.

transcript.speaker: Georgie
transcript.text: Once again, our six minutes are up, but don't forget you can test what you've learned with the worksheet on our website.

transcript.speaker: Georgie
transcript.text: Go to bbclearningenglish.com.

transcript.speaker: Phil
transcript.text: Thanks for joining us and goodbye.

transcript.speaker: Georgie
transcript.text: Goodbye!

quiz.q: What percentage of UK adults say they get less than seven hours of sleep a night? a) 15%, b) 25%, c) 35%

sentences.ko: 그런데 필, 밤에 잠을 잘 못 자서 힘들 때가 있나요?

sentences.text: Sometimes I can lie there for hours.
sentences.ko: 가끔은 몇 시간 동안 누워만 있어요.

reading.title: Is brown rice really healthier than white rice?
reading.summaryKo: 현미가 몸에 좋다는 연구는 대부분 관찰 연구라 생활습관 차이가 섞여 있어요. 실제 무작위 시험에서는 혈당 개선 효과가 뚜렷하지 않았고, 색깔보다 쌀 품종(아밀로스 함량)과 가공법(파보일링, 냉장 보관)이 더 중요하다는 글이에요.
excerpt: Rice supplies nearly a fifth of the world's calories. Which sort, though, is healthiest? Brown rice becomes white when milling removes its fibrous outer layer (known as the bran), and nutrient-rich seed embryo (the germ), so nutritional lore naturally favours the former. Indeed, some striking findings seem to support that preference. Look closer, though, and the colour of rice may not be what matters most.

Correlation, though, is not causation. People who prefer brown rice tend to smoke less, exercise more and eat healthier food overall. Although the authors of the papers from 2022 and 2010 attempted to account for such confounding lifestyle differences, they acknowledged that their findings could still be skewed. So what happens when researchers actually instruct people to eat brown rather than white rice?
reading.tip: 부제 'The scientific evidence goes against the grain'은 말장난이에요. go against the grain = 통념에 어긋나다, grain = 곡물. 임상검사실에서 일하시니 'correlation is not causation'은 업무 대화에서도 바로 쓸 수 있어요.

vocab.example: Nutritional lore naturally favours brown rice.
Some striking findings seem to support that preference.
They tried to account for confounding lifestyle differences.
Their findings could still be skewed.
Amylose content is the most consistently important determinant of how sharply rice raises blood sugar.
The scientific evidence goes against the grain.

writing.prompt: What is the article's main point? Write 1–3 sentences in English.
writing.question: Why can't observational studies prove that brown rice prevents diabetes?
writing.hint: 현미를 먹는 사람들은 담배를 덜 피우고 운동을 더 해요. 'confounding'과 'correlation is not causation'을 써 보세요.

speaking.prompt: In one minute, tell a friend whether they should switch to brown rice, and why (or why not).
speaking.alt: 쉬운 버전: What do you usually eat for dinner? Does it affect your sleep?
